patients.summary: Office manager in Holyoke with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, metabolic syndrome, stable schizophrenia on olanzapine, right knee osteoarthritis and a pack-a-day habit. Develops psoriasis, then antipsychotic-associated diabetes, then Cushing disease from an ACTH-producing pituitary adenoma that is resected, and later an NSAID-related bleeding duodenal ulcer.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
45 y/o man, office manager, here to establish. Left his old primary care office mostly because he wanted to be able to reach a doctor without a two-week wait. Records requested today.

He has had high blood pressure and high cholesterol for years, both on pills, and was told a few years ago he has metabolic syndrome. Schizophrenia has been quiet for a long time; he sees an outside psychiatrist every few months who prescribes olanzapine. Right knee aches with stairs and long days on his feet, takes ibuprofen from the drugstore a few times a week, 1-2 tabs.

Meds: lisinopril 10 daily, atorvastatin 20 daily, olanzapine 10 qhs, ibuprofen 200-400 prn.
Allergies: NKDA.
PSH: none.
FH: father lung cancer, died at 60. Mother HTN and high cholesterol.
SH: married, lives in Holyoke. Smokes about a pack a day, started at 15, ~30 pack-years. Has tried to quit before. 1-2 drinks on weekends. No drugs.

ROS: no chest pain, dyspnea, cough, hemoptysis, GI or urinary complaints. Mood ok, sleeping fine.

Exam: vitals as charted, BMI 28. Pleasant, organized, good eye contact. HEENT unremarkable. Neck supple, no thyroid enlargement. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear, no wheeze. Abdomen soft, nontender. R knee: mild crepitus, no effusion, full ROM. No edema. Skin clear.

A/P
1. HTN, at goal on lisinopril. CMP.
2. Hyperlipidemia, on atorvastatin 20. Lipids today.
3. Metabolic syndrome. A1c, weight. Talked about walking at lunch.
4. Schizophrenia, stable, psychiatry following. Will ask for a copy of their notes.
5. R knee OA. Ibuprofen sparingly, ok for now.
6. Tobacco, 1 ppd. Strongly advised to quit, not ready today. Will keep raising it.
7. HM: Tdap today. Hep C and HIV screening done today. Flu shot when it's in.

RTC 3-4 months.

documents.title: Your lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Eric, your labs from Tuesday look fine. Kidney function and potassium normal, blood count normal, A1c 5.6 which is just under the line. LDL is 100 on the atorvastatin. Hep C and HIV tests negative. Nothing to change. See you in the new year.

Repeated quit-smoking advice documented each year. No surgeries.

documents.title: Primary Care Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Routine recheck. Feels well, nothing new, taking everything as prescribed. One question: a drug rep came through his office last week, left a bag of samples of a new brand-name blood pressure pill and a glossy flyer saying it works better than the older ones. Wants to know if he should switch.

We talked it through. His pressure is where we want it on lisinopril, which is cheap, once a day, and has decades of outcome data behind it. A flyer from the company that makes the drug isn't the same as head-to-head evidence, and a new brand would cost him more for no clear gain. He was fine with that, said he figured as much. Suggested he not start the samples.

Still ~1 ppd. Not ready to set a quit date; knows the door is open.

O: BP 132/84, HR 78. Comfortable. Heart regular, lungs clear, no edema.

A/P
HTN - controlled, continue lisinopril 10. BMP today.
Hyperlipidemia - atorvastatin 20, fasting lipids today.
Tobacco - advised again.
f/u in summer for a physical.

documents.author: PCP

documents.title: Psychiatry letter
documents.author: psychiatry
documents.body:
Outpatient Psychiatry
Re: Eric Strong, DOB 02/28/1974

Dear Doctor,

Writing at your office's request to share an update. Mr. Strong has been in my care for several years for schizophrenia. He has been clinically stable for a long stretch on olanzapine 10 mg at bedtime, with no psychotic symptoms, no hospitalizations and good function at work and home. I see him every three months. No medication changes planned.

Allergies: none known.

I'd appreciate continued monitoring of weight, lipids and glucose on your end, and I'll do the same when I have labs. Please call with any concerns.

Sincerely,
Attending psychiatrist

documents.title: Video Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Video visit (pt at home, office closed to routine visits). Consent obtained.

Rash since around New Year. Started on both elbows and knees, now in his scalp and a patch on the low back. Itches a little, doesn't hurt. No new soaps, meds or detergents. No joint pain. No fever.

On camera: well-defined pink-red plaques with thick white scale over both elbows; scalp hard to see on video but he describes flaking at the hairline.

Looks like psoriasis to me. Referring to dermatology to confirm and treat; their office is seeing new patients in person again in May. Until then plain moisturizer, avoid picking at the scale.

documents.title: Dermatology consultation
documents.author: dermatology
documents.body:
Outside Dermatology Associates
Date of service: 05/04/2020
Patient: Eric Strong, 46 y/o M
Referring: Primary Care

Reason for consult: rash, four months, getting worse.

History: Lesions began on the elbows and knees in early January and have since appeared on the scalp and lower back. Mild pruritus, no pain. He denies arthralgia, fever, weight loss or any recent medication change. PMH notable for hypertension and metabolic syndrome. He says his father developed a rash like this in his middle years.

Medications: lisinopril, atorvastatin, olanzapine, ibuprofen PRN.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: current smoker, ~1 ppd.

Vitals: within normal limits.

Exam: Sharply marginated erythematous plaques topped with silvery-white scale over the extensor elbows and knees, scattered on the scalp, and on the lumbosacral back. Pitting of several fingernails. Oral and genital mucosa clear. No dactylitis, no joint swelling.

Assessment: Plaque psoriasis, limited body surface area. Nail pitting noted. No signs of psoriatic arthritis today.

Plan:
- Clobetasol 0.05% ointment BID to plaques for 2 weeks, then weekends only to maintain. Avoid face and skin folds.
- Discussed that smoking and weight can make psoriasis harder to control.
- Let us know about any joint pain or morning stiffness.
- Return in 3 months or sooner.

Thank you for this referral.
Dermatology

- Lipids/A1c/CMP drawn.
- Psoriasis per derm, better.

- Mood screen negative.
- Colon cancer screening: discussed, he'd rather wait until things settle down with COVID. Revisit next year.

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
47M here for his regular check on BP and cholesterol. Psoriasis is managed by dermatology and quiet on weekend clobetasol.

No complaints. What's on his mind is lung cancer. He read an article online tying cigarettes to lung cancer, and it talked about risk going up with the dose, which got him thinking about his own numbers. His dad got a lung cancer diagnosis at 55 and died of it at 60. He's smoked about a pack a day since he was 15.

Went over it in plain terms: the more cigarettes a day and the more years, the higher the risk, and it isn't a threshold thing - every pack-year adds. The good news side of the same curve is that risk starts coming down after quitting and keeps dropping the longer he stays off. He listened closely. Not ready to pick a date, but said this is the first time he's really thought about it. CT screening for lung cancer starts at 50 for people with his history; we'll set that up when he's eligible.

Meds: lisinopril 10, atorvastatin 20, olanzapine 10 qhs (psych), ibuprofen prn knee, clobetasol oint.
NKDA.

Exam: BP 130/85, HR 78, RR 16. No distress. No cervical or supraclavicular nodes. Lungs clear throughout, good air movement. Heart regular. No clubbing. Knee unchanged.

A/P
- HTN: fine, continue lisinopril.
- Lipids: fasting panel today on atorvastatin 20.
- CBC today.
- Tobacco: as above. Offered help any time - meds, quit line, both.
- COVID vaccine: eligible now, he's booked at the pharmacy next week.
- Colon screening: he'd like to do it after the summer.

documents.title: Your results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Blood count is normal. Cholesterol: LDL 120, HDL 45, triglycerides 250. The triglycerides jumped since last year - sweets, white bread and beer all push that number. Worth cutting back where you can. We'll recheck at your physical.

documents.title: Smoking Cessation Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seeing him today for my colleague. 47 y/o with HTN, high cholesterol, metabolic syndrome, schizophrenia (stable), here because he wants to quit smoking - follows on from the April conversation about lung cancer.

Still 1 ppd, has been since he was 15. Tried patches and gum more than once; each time the cravings and the irritability got him and he was back within a few weeks. Says this time he means it: he just became a grandfather and wants to be around and healthy. Two things matter to him: he doesn't want to put on weight, and he doesn't want anything that messes with his sleep - a friend told him one of the quit pills gives you awful dreams.

Screening: no depression now, no seizures ever, no eating disorder. Schizophrenia has been stable for years on olanzapine with his psychiatrist. No head injury. BP and cholesterol controlled on his meds. Drinks socially, weekends.

Exam: vitals as charted, BMI 28. Alert, engaged, linear. Lungs clear.

A/P
Tobacco dependence, motivated.
- Bupropion XL 150 mg each morning. Talked about how it works on cravings, tends not to add weight, and taking it in the morning keeps it away from bedtime. Quit date in about 10 days once it's on board.
- Pair with the quit line; number given. Plan for triggers (first cigarette with coffee, the drive home).
- Will let his psychiatrist know he's starting it.
- RN call in a month.
- Flu shot today.

BP/lipids: no changes.

documents.title: Message to psychiatry
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Left a voicemail and faxed a note to his psychiatrist: started bupropion XL 150 daily today for smoking cessation, olanzapine unchanged, asked them to call if they have concerns.

documents.title: Cessation follow-up call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Called as planned. On bupropion XL 150 each morning, no side effects, sleeping fine, mood steady. Didn't make it all the way on his quit date but is down to about 10 cigarettes a day from a pack. Hardest time is after work. Encouraged, reviewed quit line, he hasn't called yet. Will keep going and see PCP in December.

documents.title: Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Back on the cigarettes, close to a pack a day again. Did well through mid-November at around 10 a day, then work got busy before the holidays and it crept back. Feels the bupropion isn't doing anything at this point and doesn't want to keep paying for it. Not up for another try right now - maybe after the new year, he says.

No side effects from it. Mood fine.

Vitals as charted.

Plan: stop bupropion. No shame in a relapse; most people need several attempts. Will check in each visit. Ok to restart this or try something else whenever he wants.

Colon cancer screening - he's ready now. Referral to GI for screening colonoscopy, no family history of colon cancer, no symptoms.

documents.title: Endocrinology consultation
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Endocrinology Clinic
Date of visit: 10/07/2022
Re: Eric Strong, 48 y/o man

Dear Doctor,

Thank you for asking me to see Mr. Strong about the metabolic effects of his olanzapine. He has taken olanzapine for schizophrenia for years, stable, through his psychiatrist, and carries diagnoses of metabolic syndrome, hypertension and hyperlipidemia.

Over the past three months he has been thirsty much of the time and urinating more often, including at night, and has gained about 10 pounds over the same stretch. He has not changed what he eats or how active he is. His mother has type 2 diabetes.

Medications: lisinopril 10 mg once daily, atorvastatin 20 mg once daily, ibuprofen 200-400 mg as needed for knee pain.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: smokes about a pack a day since age 15, roughly 30 pack-years. Social alcohol, 1-2 drinks on weekends. Office manager.

Exam: BP 135/85. BMI 32. He has a cushingoid appearance. Otherwise unremarkable.

Fasting labs this morning: glucose 126 mg/dL and A1c 7.2%. Total cholesterol 230, HDL 35, triglycerides 250, LDL 145 mg/dL.

Assessment:
1. Type 2 diabetes, new, in the setting of olanzapine and metabolic syndrome - antipsychotic-induced. Symptomatic hyperglycemia but A1c 7.2.
2. Obesity, BMI 32.
3. Dyslipidemia, as above.

Plan:
- Metformin 500 mg twice daily with meals; we'll titrate at the next visit.
- Met with our diabetes educator today to go over food choices.
- Return in 3 months with an A1c.

I will keep you informed.

Sincerely,
Endocrinology

Follow-up for BP, cholesterol, smoking, and the diabetes endocrinology is co-managing. Missed the July slot, rescheduled. Says he feels fine, no complaints.

He wanted to spend time on smoking and his health. Which diseases is he actually at risk for? Went through it: heart attack and stroke (stacked on top of diabetes, BP and cholesterol), COPD, and cancers - lung most of all, also bladder, throat, mouth. Lung cancer is the one that scares him; his dad died of it at 60. He has read a lot about how the smoking link was worked out and wanted to talk it through, which we did. He's 49; CT screening for lung cancer starts at 50 and he turns 50 in February - he wants it. Will do a screening visit after his birthday and order the CT.

Still a pack a day. Not ready to quit. Did ask whether the quit pill could be tried again some time - yes, any time.

NKDA.

- Lipids/A1c/BMP/CBC today.
- T2DM: on metformin.
- Tobacco: as above; lung screening in Feb/March.
- Vaccines: flu, PCV20, updated COVID today.

documents.title: Lung Screening Shared Decision Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Video visit, pt at his office on lunch break, identity confirmed.

Turned 50 last week. Current smoker, a pack a day since 15 = 35 pack-years. No cough change, no hemoptysis, no weight loss. Father died of lung cancer at 60.

Shared decision-making done with the decision aid: benefits (finding cancer early), harms (false positives, follow-up scans, rare biopsies, radiation dose), annual scans as long as eligible, and that screening is not a substitute for quitting. He wants to go ahead.

Cessation counseling again; open to revisiting meds later this year.

Plan: LDCT ordered.

reports.study: Low-dose CT chest for lung cancer screening
reports.text:
Indication: annual lung cancer screening. Current smoker, 35 pack-years.
Technique: low-dose noncontrast CT of the chest.
Comparison: none.
Findings: Lungs are clear. No pulmonary nodules. Airways patent. No pleural effusion. Heart size normal. No mediastinal or hilar adenopathy. Visualized upper abdomen unremarkable. No suspicious osseous lesion.
reports.conclusion: Lung-RADS 1: negative. Continue annual screening with low-dose CT in 12 months.

documents.title: CT result
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Your lung screening CT was clear - no nodules. That's the best result. We repeat it every year. The single best thing for your lungs is still quitting, and I'm here when you're ready.

- HTN on lisinopril.
- Lipids today.
- Tobacco: counseled.

documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Endocrinology Clinic - visit 10/07/2024 (dictated 10/07/2024)
Re: Eric Strong, 50 y/o man

Dear Doctor,

I saw Mr. Strong back for his diabetes, and he came in with a different story this time. Over several months he has kept gaining weight and feels worn out. His belly has grown and his face has filled out, though nothing about how he eats or exercises has changed. His wife, who came with him, says he's been more irritable lately and noticed purple stretch marks on his stomach. He has no headaches, no change in vision, no nipple discharge.

Medications: metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 10 mg, atorvastatin 20 mg, olanzapine 10 mg at bedtime, ibuprofen 200-400 mg prn knee.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: pack a day since 15. Weekend drinks.

Exam: BP 156/92. Weight 107.7 kg, BMI 34. Round, plethoric face. Abdomen obese with broad violaceous striae. Proximal weakness in both arms and legs. Point tenderness over the lumbar spine.

A lumbar spine film today shows an L1 compression fracture.

Assessment: the picture is strongly suggestive of hypercortisolism (Cushing syndrome), with a fragility fracture and a rise in BP and glucose. A1c today 7.4%.

Plan:
- Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test, ACTH, 24-hour urine free cortisol, vitamin D. Instructions given.
- Further imaging depending on results.
- Back: avoid heavy lifting. 
- I'll write again with results.

Sincerely,
Endocrinology

documents.title: Cortisol tests
documents.author: patient
documents.body: The endocrinologist thinks my body might be making too much cortisol and found a fracture in my back. I did the pill test and the urine jug. Should I be worried? My wife is pretty worried.

documents.title: Reply
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Eric - I saw her note. It makes sense to check, because too much cortisol would explain a lot of what you've been dealing with, and it is treatable. Let's wait for the results before worrying; she'll send them to both of us and I'll call you once I've seen them. Meanwhile no heavy lifting with that back. Your appointment here is 10/31.

reports.study: MRI pituitary with and without contrast
reports.text:
Indication: ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism.
Technique: dedicated thin-section sellar imaging, pre- and post-gadolinium, including dynamic post-contrast sequences.
Findings: 10 mm hypoenhancing lesion in the right side of the pituitary gland, measured in the coronal plane on dynamic images. No extension into the cavernous sinus; the cavernous carotids are normal. Optic chiasm clear of the gland and normal in appearance. Infundibulum midline. Sella normal size. Visualized brain unremarkable.
reports.conclusion: 10 mm right-sided pituitary lesion, consistent with adenoma in this clinical setting. No cavernous sinus invasion; optic chiasm clear.

medications.sig: Take 1 tablet (1000 units) by mouth daily

documents.title: Endocrinology results
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Endocrinology Clinic
Re: Eric Strong

Dear Doctor,

Following up on my letter of 10/07 with results.

- Cortisol after 1 mg overnight dexamethasone: 9.6 ug/dL (normal suppression under 1.8)
- 24-hour urine free cortisol: 286 ug/24 h (reference under 50)
- ACTH: 84 pg/mL (reference 7-63)
- Potassium 3.9. A1c 7.4%.
- 25-hydroxyvitamin D: 21 ng/mL

This confirms ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome. Pituitary MRI on 10/21 shows a 10 mm right-sided pituitary adenoma without cavernous sinus invasion, chiasm clear. Together: Cushing disease from an ACTH-producing pituitary adenoma.

Plan:
- Referral to pituitary neurosurgery for transsphenoidal resection; their office will call him.
- DXA scan given the L1 fracture - ordered.
- Vitamin D3 1000 units daily, and calcium from food (2-3 dairy servings a day).
- Metformin unchanged for now; glucose should improve once the cortisol is treated.
- I spoke with him by phone today and he understands the plan.

Allergies: NKDA.

Sincerely,
Endocrinology

documents.title: Call with patient
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Called Eric after reading the endocrinology letter. He'd already heard from them. Explained in plain words that a small benign growth in the pituitary is making the hormone that drives his body to overproduce cortisol, and that this explains the weight, the stretch marks, the weakness, the back fracture and the higher sugars and BP. Surgery through the nose is the usual treatment and usually works. He was relieved there's a reason. Keeping his appointment here Thursday.

Pituitary and Skull Base Neurosurgery, academic medical center
Date of visit: 11/19/2024
Re: Eric Strong, 50M

Referred by endocrinology for Cushing disease. Biochemistry shows ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism, and the MRI shows a 10 mm right-sided pituitary adenoma, no cavernous sinus invasion, chiasm clear. Fatigue, weight gain, proximal weakness, striae; L1 compression fracture. No headache or visual complaints.

Academic medical center - Neurosurgery
Admitted 12/10/2024, discharged 12/13/2024
Patient: Eric Strong, 50M

Diagnosis: Cushing disease, ACTH-producing pituitary adenoma.
Procedure 12/10: endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal resection of pituitary adenoma. Uncomplicated. No intraoperative CSF leak.

Course: steroids were held after surgery to assess remission. Morning cortisol on 12/12 was 1.2 ug/dL, consistent with surgical remission; hydrocortisone replacement started. Sodium stayed normal and urine output normal throughout - no diabetes insipidus. Glucose managed with home metformin. Walking independently.

Discharge medications: hydrocortisone 10 mg twice daily (NEW; sick-day rules taught - double for fever or vomiting, emergency care for vomiting that won't stop), metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 10 mg qd, atorvastatin 20 mg qd, olanzapine 10 mg qhs, vitamin D3 1000 units daily.
Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: endocrinology in 6-8 weeks, neurosurgery in 3 weeks, PCP within a week. No nose blowing, straining or heavy lifting for 4 weeks.
Pathology: ACTH-positive pituitary adenoma.

Feels washed out and achy, which he was warned about as the cortisol comes down. Appetite lower. Nose congested, no clear drip, no headache, vision fine. Not overly thirsty. Back about the same. Still smoking about a pack a day.

Meds reconciled: hydrocortisone 10 BID, metformin 1000 BID, lisinopril 10, atorvastatin 20, olanzapine 10 qhs, vitamin D3, ibuprofen prn knee.

Exam: vitals as charted, weight 105.7 (down 2 kg). Alert, tired. Nares with crusting, no discharge. Visual fields full. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Abdomen striae unchanged.

A/P
- s/p resection, early remission on replacement steroids. Sick-day rules reviewed again; letter for his wallet. Endocrinology follow-up 2/4.
- T2DM: watch for lows as cortisol falls; call if fasting sugars under 80.
- BP on lisinopril, expect it to come down.

Endocrinology Clinic - 02/04/2025
Re: Eric Strong

Dear Doctor,

Mr. Strong is eight weeks past transsphenoidal resection of his ACTH-staining adenoma. The post-operative morning cortisol of 1.2 ug/dL indicates remission. He feels better week by week; weight is down to 103 kg. No symptoms of under-replacement.

Current: hydrocortisone 10 mg twice daily, metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 10, atorvastatin 20, olanzapine 10 qhs, vitamin D3 1000 units. NKDA.

Plan:
- Reduce hydrocortisone to 10 mg each morning only. Sick-day rules unchanged.
- I'll check a morning cortisol off hydrocortisone in a few months to see if his own adrenal function has recovered.
- Bone: DXA showed low bone mass (L2-L4 T -2.2, femoral neck -1.7, total hip -1.3). Bone density usually recovers substantially once cortisol is normal, so I'll hold off on bone medication and repeat DXA a year after remission, around November 2026. Continue vitamin D and dietary calcium.
- Diabetes: metformin unchanged.

Sincerely,
Endocrinology

Emergency Department, community hospital
Seen 10/17/2025
Patient: Eric Strong, 51M

CC: black stools, upper abdominal pain.

HPI: Black, tarry stools for two days with a dull, gnawing ache in the upper abdomen that wakes him at night. Eating eases it for a while, then it comes back worse. No vomiting, no blood in vomit, no lightheadedness at rest. History of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, metabolic syndrome, schizophrenia and an ACTH-producing pituitary adenoma. Takes lisinopril and atorvastatin, olanzapine 10 mg nightly, and uses over-the-counter ibuprofen now and then for chronic knee pain.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: current smoker, about a pack a day since 15. Weekend alcohol, 1-2 drinks. Office manager.
Family: father died of lung cancer at 60; mother with hypertension and hyperlipidemia.

Exam: BP 130/85, HR 98. Pale. Abdomen soft with mild epigastric tenderness, no rebound, no guarding. Rectal: black stool, guaiac positive.

Labs: hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, hematocrit 30.5%, MCV 86 fL. BUN 29, creatinine 1.0. Liver enzymes normal. INR normal.

ED course: two large-bore IVs, IV pantoprazole bolus and infusion. Ibuprofen held. GI consulted. Heart rate down to 90 on reassessment. No transfusion needed.

Impression: upper GI bleed, likely peptic ulcer in setting of NSAID use.
Disposition: admitted to medicine for endoscopy.

reports.text:
Specimen: gastric antrum and body biopsies.
Microscopic: gastric mucosa without significant inflammation. No Helicobacter pylori organisms identified on routine and immunohistochemical staining. No intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia or malignancy.
reports.conclusion: Gastric mucosa, negative for Helicobacter pylori. No dysplasia or malignancy.
